title: interim-scratch-nat44-sni-fallthrough
content:
Purpose:
Quick scratchpad capturing commands, traces, and hypotheses from the week-long private-deploy egress flakiness. Trying to capture a minimal reproducer and a prioritized next-step list. Primary symptom: intermittent TLS handshake failures to external vendor endpoints when traffic egresses via peered VPC -> transit path -> NAT Gateway. Failures look like either TLS-level aborts or immediate TCP RST depending on client and time of day.

Observed behaviour (high level):
- App instances inside customer VPC (private-deploy cluster) occasionally fail outbound HTTPS calls to vendor.api.example.com. Fail rate ~0.5-2% per minute under steady load; spikes during burst.
- Failures present as either: (A) "tls: first record does not look like a TLS handshake" at the app, or (B) connection reset after SYN/ACK (server or intermediate resets), or (C) successful TCP 3-way but TLS verification fails with certificate CN mismatch (rare).
- Curl from bastion in same subnet mostly succeeds. Curl from app pod sometimes fails — points to path asymmetry or ephemeral port exhaustion/NAT mapping weirdness.

Commands I ran (raw):
- Resolve and direct connect probes: 
  - curl -v --resolve vendor.api.example.com:443:203.0.113.12 https://vendor.api.example.com/health --connect-to vendor.api.example.com:443:203.0.113.12
  - openssl s_client -connect 203.0.113.12:443 -servername vendor.api.example.com -brief
  - openssl s_client -connect 198.51.100.45:443 -servername vendor.api.example.com -brief  (tested vendor public IPs vs egress NAT IPs)
- Native captures on pod host and at NAT: 
  - sudo tcpdump -i eth0 -w /tmp/pod-eth0.pcap host 203.0.113.12 and port 443
  - sudo tcpdump -i gw-eni -w /tmp/gw-to-vendor.pcap host 203.0.113.12 and port 443
- Socket table and conntrack checks:
  - ss -tanp | grep 203.0.113.12
  - sudo conntrack -L | grep 203.0.113.12
- Routing checks (pod host): 
  - ip route get 203.0.113.12
  - ip rule show; ip route show table 100 (the peering-specific table)
- Iptables/ebtables: 
  - sudo iptables-save > /tmp/iptables-save.txt
  - sudo nft list ruleset (some nodes use nft)
- MTU checks: 
  - ping -M do -s 1472 203.0.113.12 (fragmentation test)

Key snippets pulled from captures/outputs: (trimmed)
- App log: "error: tls: first record does not look like a TLS handshake" on POST /v1/predict
- tcpdump (pod-host) around failure event: 
  12:02:13.123456 IP 10.32.5.12.40132 > 203.0.113.12.443: Flags [S], seq 12345678, win 64240, options [mss 1460,sackOK,TS val 123 ecr 0,nop,wscale 7], length 0
  12:02:13.123789 IP 203.0.113.12.443 > 10.32.5.12.40132: Flags [S.], seq 87654321, ack 12345679, win 65535, options [mss 1460,sackOK,TS val 456 ecr 123], length 0
  12:02:13.124012 IP 10.32.5.12.40132 > 203.0.113.12.443: Flags [.], ack 1, win 502, length 0
  12:02:13.234567 IP 10.32.5.12.40132 > 203.0.113.12.443: Flags [P.], seq 1:517, ack 1, win 502, length 516
  12:02:13.234890 IP 203.0.113.12.443 > 10.32.5.12.40132: RST, seq 2, win 0, length 0
- tcpdump at NAT (same timeframe): we see forwarded packets from egress IP 198.51.100.45:40132 to vendor 203.0.113.12:443; server RST back to 198.51.100.45 occurs.
- conntrack entry TTLs for nat mapping: seen ephemeral port reuse where mapping was short-lived and reused quickly under load.

Hypotheses (ranked):
1) Asymmetric routing: some responses from vendor are returning to a different public IP (e.g., via a different NAT GW or transit provider) which the NAT table doesn't have mapping for -> RST or silence at our side. Evidence: intermittent success correlates with which NAT/GW was chosen; tcpdump at NAT shows some RSTs inbound with dst ip != mapping.
2) NAT44 ephemeral port collisions: under high connection churn the NAT mapping gets reassigned while server still has TCP state -> server RSTs. Evidence: conntrack shows mapping churn and short lifetimes under load bursts.
3) Vendor-side SNI / TLS routing to different backend: when SNI != expected (due to DNS+peering mismatch) the endpoint may route to an internal admin port that responds with RST/cleartext. Evidence: rare CN mismatch logs, and successful curl with --resolve sometimes hits different backends.
4) Path MTU/fragmentation causing vendor server to reject first TLS record as non-TLS: less likely but will test.

Quick repro recipe I used:
1) From app pod: curl -v https://vendor.api.example.com/health  (most runs succeed)
2) Run a loop to increase ephemeral churn: for i in {1..2000}; do curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}\n" https://vendor.api.example.com/health & done (one-shot concurrency)
3) Watch conntrack and tcpdump on egress; reproduce RST patterns.

Quick mitigations tested (results):
- Pin outbound SNAT to a single NAT Gateway (route table / source nat): decreased failure rate but not zero. Suggests multi-NAT path asymmetry contributes.
- Increase conntrack timeouts for ESTABLISHED and TCP transient states: marginal improvement.
- Client keepalive tune (reuse connections) strongly reduces failures (suggests NAT churn).

Next steps (practical):
- Short term: force a single egress path for private-deploy tenants that see this (route/ENI policy) and monitor reductions (owned by infra ops).
- Mid term: add flow-logging cross-check to detect response-to-unmapped-IP (Flow logs + NAT mapping join) — can create alert when vendor returns to unexpected public IP.
- Long term: work with vendor to confirm their egress/load-balancer behavior for our IP ranges (ask for a stable anycast or require SNI enforcement to avoid backend routing ambiguity).
- Also: instrument app to prefer keep-alive reuse (connection pooling) as immediate app-level mitigation.

Notes / thoughts to follow up:
- Need to capture pcap on both sides of transit (customer VPC and transit provider) at same timestamp to conclusively show asymmetry.
- Consider enabling deterministic source ports for a short window to test collision hypothesis (iptables --randomize-ports off and set base port?) — only for controlled experiments.
- Check whether any intermediate inspection proxies (partner peering) perform TLS interception; that would explain non-TLS first-record errors.

Attachments/where to find traces: /shared/troubleshooting/egress-pcaps/2025-06-18-19-12 (internal), slack-thread #private-egress-incident-4127.

Unresolved questions:
- Is there a time-of-day pattern matching vendor backend scaling? 
- Are NAT gateway health checks or auto-scaling replacing instances and causing mapping flaps?

If anyone else wants to pick this up: start with "pin egress to single NAT" experiment and the conntrack logging during a replay load. I'll try to capture a synchronized pcap next maintenance window.

-- Morgan
